steps.calloutTitle: Laxmi Sunrise Bank · Sujata's compliance workbench
steps.calloutText: Every loan officer sees their assigned loans with both ESRM and Green Finance Taxonomy status in one place. Full audit trail underneath.
steps.narration: Welcome. This is the compliance workbench built for Laxmi Sunrise Bank. Sujata Adhikari is a loan officer. Her queue shows every loan Laxmi has assigned to her, with both regulatory obligations visible on one row. The Nepal Rastra Bank ESRM screening from the 2018 directive, and the Green Finance Taxonomy classification from the October 2024 directive. Over the next six minutes I will walk you through how Sujata completes both flows on a single loan, step by step.

steps.calloutText: ESDD checklist status. Taxonomy classification. Both visible before Sujata clicks in.
steps.narration: Each card in Sujata's queue represents one loan. She sees at a glance where each regulatory flow stands. The ESDD checklist progress or risk chip, and the taxonomy classification color if the sector is eligible. Two independent action buttons let her pick which flow to work on next. The platform does not force an order.

steps.calloutText: Prefilled from the loan record. NRB Annex 5 requires these fields at the top of every checklist.
steps.narration: When Sujata opens the ESDD checklist, the first step is basic information. Date, transaction ID, client name, industry, location. All prefilled from the loan record. NRB Annex 5 requires these fields at the top of every ESDD file. She confirms and moves on.

steps.calloutText: Three questions on legal issues, stakeholder grievances, and sensitive-area siting. Verbatim NRB language.
steps.narration: Section 1. General Risk. Three questions on legal permits and standing, stakeholder grievances or media coverage, and whether the site sits near protected or sensitive areas. Each question offers four options. A is the best case. B is partial mitigation with a plan. C is an unmitigated concern that will trigger escalation. D is not applicable. The wording matches the 2018 NRB directive verbatim so the audit trail is defensible.

steps.calloutText: Four questions on air, water, land pollution, and energy efficiency.
steps.narration: Section 2. Environmental health and safety. Four questions on air and noise pollution, water pollution, land pollution and waste handling, and energy efficiency or renewables. Each carries its own guidance notes drawn from the NRB source document, so the officer knows what evidence to look for. Every answer auto-saves the moment Sujata clicks it, timestamped and attributed to her officer identity.

steps.calloutTitle: Section 3 · Social Risks · the escalation triggers
steps.calloutText: Four questions on occupational H&S, labour practices, community H&S, and stakeholder consultation. Two 'c' answers here drive the credit-committee escalation.
steps.narration: Section 3. Social risks. Four questions on occupational health and safety, labour practices, community health and safety, and stakeholder consultation with indigenous peoples. On this loan the officer recorded a 'c' answer to labour practices and another to community health and safety. Those two answers are what triggered the credit-committee escalation you saw in the queue. Every question includes NRB's own guidance notes and a free-text remarks field for evidence references.

steps.calloutText: Three sector-specific questions layered on top of the 11 core questions. Different sectors get different supplements.
steps.narration: Section 4. This is the cement sector supplement. Three additional questions specific to cement operations. Kiln stack particulate emissions, limestone quarry rehabilitation, and fugitive dust from clinker handling and haul roads. Different sectors get different supplements. Hydropower gets four hydro-specific questions. Brick kilns get four questions including the automatic escalation on child or bonded labour. Textiles, steel, chemicals, and agriculture each have their own set. Sujata only sees the supplement that applies to this loan's sector.

steps.calloutText: Scoring engine derives risk class and recommendation. Escalation banner surfaces the driving questions.
steps.narration: The review step. The scoring engine runs the NRB rules over Sujata's answers and produces a risk class and recommendation. On this loan the two 'c' answers in Section 3 triggered the escalation. The rationale text spells out exactly why. The recommendation is approve with conditions plus binding covenants on the flagged items and quarterly monitoring. Save the screening and it is in the audit trail. The manager sees it immediately.

steps.calloutText: Same loan, second regulatory flow. NRB Green Finance Taxonomy from October 2024.
steps.narration: Now the second regulatory flow. The Green Finance Taxonomy from NRB October 2024. Sujata opens the taxonomy wizard for the same cement loan. Step 1 is loan basics, prefilled from the loan record. She confirms and moves on to activity selection.

steps.calloutText: 10 activities encoded from NRB Oct 2024. Suggested activities appear first based on the borrower's sector.
steps.narration: Step 2. Choose the applicable activity. The wizard suggests activities based on the borrower's sector. For a cement borrower with waste heat recovery, that is the cement-with-WHR activity. Ten activities are encoded from the October 2024 directive covering the Nepal cases banks most commonly underwrite. Hydropower at three capacity tiers. Utility solar. Cement with WHR. Green buildings. Organic agriculture. Electric vehicles. High-efficiency irrigation. And the fossil-fuel exclusion.

steps.calloutTitle: Step 3 · Criteria plus central DNSH library
steps.calloutText: Activity-specific questions plus shared 'Do No Significant Harm' checks pulled from a central library.
steps.narration: Step 3. Each activity carries its own criteria plus a set of shared Do No Significant Harm checks. DNSH is the taxonomy principle that says an activity cannot count as green if it materially harms another environmental objective. Water. Biodiversity. Community rights. Climate adaptation. The DNSH checks live in a central library so the same check, for example environmental flow or resettlement discharged, is defined once and referenced by every activity that uses it. No drift between activities, no re-encoding when new activities land.

steps.calloutText: Live preview of the derivation. Save records the classification, rationale, and citation to the audit trail.
steps.narration: Step 4. Review and save. The classifier returns Green, Amber, or Red with any DNSH failures called out separately. Cement with waste heat recovery lands on Amber, transitional financing, because cement remains a hard-to-abate sector under NRB's own methodology. Sujata sees a live preview before she saves. The saved classification carries the rationale text and the NRB citation so the audit trail is defensible.

steps.calloutText: Sujata's card now shows the risk chip on the ESDD side and the Amber classification on the Taxonomy side.
steps.narration: Back in her queue. The loan card now shows both regulatory decisions. A risk chip on the ESDD side and an Amber classification on the Taxonomy side. The manager's view updates immediately because both surfaces read from the same records. Sujata moves on to her next loan.

steps.calloutTitle: Two regulations, one workflow, full attribution
steps.calloutText: ESRM Annex 5. Green Finance Taxonomy. Every capture officer-attributed and timestamped.
steps.narration: That is the officer workflow. Two Nepal Rastra Bank regulations captured verbatim, one workspace, every answer attributed to Sujata's officer identity, every classification carrying its NRB citation. When the compliance manager reviews her work, or NRB examines the loan three years from now, the audit trail is complete. Thanks for watching.
